No `const` for simple types

This "smells" a lot like C++'s string_view, if you agree maybe we should just add that concept to our codebase, it would really just require adding a handful of start/end pointers to the range, and some non-owning ctors etc for our other String classes?
Should we have operator+(const StrRange)() as well? One of the more common things we see is "String()" + "static_string". We could avoid a copy there, as well as a strlen().
Actually, never mind. This is right now just a reuse of the old concept. I will make a PR when this is merged to add that to this.
Oh yeah, I suppose that's a good idea. I'll get on that.

We've had a little exchange over this in https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11249. I'd be fine with using `std::string_view`. I went for `StrRange` instead since it already existed, and because `std::string_view` would be the first use of STL in the entire code base, so I was concerned it may be some kind of hard rule to avoid it.

Probably also for operator==() if it isn't there yet, "some String() == "static_string" is also very common. I don't know if it makes sense to also plumb it through for begins_with() and stuff. If we don't have it yet. We really need to try to avoid making a lot of temporary Strings for no good reason! :)

I was hoping to address all the non-constructor functions in future PRs. A lot of these functions are duplicated for no reason, to be able to accept both `String` and `const char *`, so trying to address them all here will be a huge refactor and increase the barrier to merge. Better to proceed in small steps, I think. Thinking about it, `operator+=` is also probably better avoided for now, just to be able to move more quickly with merging this one.
Alright, fair enough.
Does copy_from_unchecked does not handle the 0 length correctly ?
if... else if ...else so you can remove `continue`s would be clearer ?
if `p_clip_to_len` was unsigned, no need for the if
I would have used a more explicit uint64 type. No need to use uint32 as it will be padded anyway. So it will be clearer that every size is supported.
you should give length, even if we do not know if it is faster in this implementation, future implementations could make it faster, and it definitely can't be slower knowing the size.
same
Yep, it doesn't.

I disagree, I think early return / early continue is more readable code, at least in the case where the early returns are less 'important' than the default case. But in any case, the code was already written like that, so I think it's outside the scope of the PR to reformat it.

Yeah, the function has a strange design, but I don't think I should change its behavior now. It's just extracted from earlier `copy_from` implementations, and expects that people may throw in a `-1` to skip the length check.

In the long run i'd like to remove the whole `p_clip_to` functionality completely anyway, since there's no good reason to have it. But that's outside the scope of this PR.
You mean use `uint64` instead of `size_t`? That would be fairly unusual when dealing with arrays.

Hrm, I guess that's true. I also misunderstood the way it's used, so i was additionally hesitant to input it. 

(Ideally `parse_utf16` would be reformatted to take a `StrRange`, but that's outside the scope of this PR)
even if they throw a -1, it will work with unsigned as it will cast it to its maxValue and be stopped by length. But yeah, if it is like that in other places, consistency is good.

Again, stylistic. But it removes ambiguity. 
Unusual where ? CowData use uint64_t for its size, LocalVector uses uint32_t
There is no `len` to pass into here, it needs to be parsed to find `NULL`.
Just a stylistic proposition. the code will be the same, so feel free to resolve.

Interesting. I'm not sure why that is. Possibly because they're designed to be easily exposeable to GDScript? 
Still, I think `size_t` is cleaner; it's very common to use that for sizes across c++.

I know that it is the default in C++ standard library. It's just, why be ambiguous on the size of a type when you don't have to. Size_t probably always is 64bits nowadays anyway, this is why this is a style choice. Any choice will do, just raising a point :).
my bad :(
I'll keep it as `size_t` for now. But let's keep the discussion open for other people to chime in!

Style changes in core are inherently a **very** low priority, so I'm not too surprised there's mixing and matching of different names/formats. A lot of the discrepancies could come down to how several templates originally used `int`/32-bit storage logic instead of 64-bit, but I can't say for certain. In any case, `size_t` is perfectly acceptable, and is arguably the best option for logic/metrics having to deal with… Well, size!
